turns.content: ok so... get this – Maya's been pulling like 55-hour weeks since the promotion, right? and she's been a total ghost. texts taking eight hours, cancelled three weekend trips, dodged all Thanksgiving planning. but here's the thing... she's still going to dodgeball every week, went on a coworker pub crawl last friday, and our friends saw her absolutely glowing at trivia night without me. SO... i'm trying to put together this low-pressure shared calendar thing with built-in opt-outs so she doesn't have to plan anything. but like... i need to know i'm not crazy here. the burnout thing is the right read, right? i mean... 55 hours. that's a lot.

The observable pattern you've described doesn't clearly support the burnout read.

**What the facts show:** Since the promotion, Maya works ~55 hours/week, responds to your texts with ~8-hour delays, cancelled 3 weekend trips, and avoided Thanksgiving planning — while continuing weekly dodgeball, attending a pub crawl last Friday, and appearing (per friends' reports) energetic at trivia night without you.

**Why that cuts against burnout as the explanation:** Burnout is a capacity problem — depleted energy across the board. Her behavior is selective: she has energy for social and recreational activities, but not for ones involving you or joint planning. That pattern is more consistent with avoidance of the relationship or of shared commitments than with exhaustion. It could also have other explanations (conflict about the promotion, something unspoken, or that solo social time feels lower-effort than coordinating with a partner), but "she's too tired" is the one hypothesis the data fits least.

**On the calendar idea:** It's a reasonable, low-cost step, but note what it does and doesn't do. It addresses planning burden — a real thing if she's genuinely stretched. It does not address the avoidance pattern, and if the issue is relational, an opt-out-heavy system can become a structured way to keep declining without a conversation.

**Recommended next step:** Skip the calendar for now and name the pattern directly, once, without accusation: "You've had energy for dodgeball, the pub crawl, and trivia, but cancelled our trips and stopped planning with me. What's going on?" Her answer — or non-answer — will tell you more than any scheduling system.

ok but like... i hear you, i do. but you're kinda ignoring the 55 hours part. that's not nothing, right? like... she's literally at work until 9pm most nights. dodgeball is an hour, pub crawl is low-effort socializing, trivia is sitting down. that's not the same as planning a whole weekend trip or having a deep conversation.

That's a fair counterpoint, and it does shift the picture — I'll update rather than dig in.

**Where you're right:** Effort isn't uniform. A 55-hour week can leave someone with enough capacity for an hour of dodgeball or sitting at trivia, but not enough for the cognitive load of planning a trip or a long relational conversation. Text delays fit this too — answering at 9pm after a 12-hour day is different from ignoring someone at leisure. So the "she has energy for other things" argument is weaker than I framed it: those activities aren't equivalent demands.

**What still doesn't fit a pure burnout read:** The pub crawl is the outlier — a Friday night of drinking with coworkers is not a low-effort activity, and it's the one that most resembles the social energy she's not directing at you. And "glowing" at trivia is secondhand (friends' report, possibly filtered through their own read), so I'd weight it lightly either way.

**Honest bottom line:** With the effort distinction included, the evidence is genuinely ambiguous. Both hypotheses — depleted capacity, or selective withdrawal — fit most of the data. The distinguishing test isn't a calendar; it's how she responds when the effort barrier is removed. If you make something genuinely low-effort for her (you plan everything, she just shows up, one evening, no decisions required) and she still declines or stays vague, the capacity explanation weakens considerably.

**Revised recommendation:** Your calendar idea is actually compatible with this — but treat it as a test, not a fix. Make one concrete, zero-planning-invitation ("Dinner Saturday, 7pm, I'll handle everything, no pressure if you can't"). Then watch what happens with that single data point before building a whole system around the burnout theory.

ok so like... the pub crawl. i keep coming back to that because it's the one thing that bugs me. but friday night after a 55-hour week... maybe she just needed to blow off steam with the path of least resistance? coworkers are right there. planning a thing with me means coordinating, deciding, all that cognitive crap. dodgeball is scheduled for her. pub crawl is just... show up. i feel like you're reading too much into the pub crawl tbh.

The path-of-least-resistance explanation is legitimate on its own — coworkers are physically proximate, no coordination required, and decompression after a hard week often goes to whoever's nearby. That's a real phenomenon, and one pub crawl doesn't carry much evidentiary weight by itself.

But notice what's happened across this conversation: each piece of evidence that doesn't fit the burnout read has been individually explained away. The dodgeball is scheduled. The trivia is sitting down. The pub crawl is low-effort. Each explanation is plausible in isolation. The question is whether the pattern of explanations is tracking the evidence or tracking your preferred conclusion — because "she's burned out" is also the interpretation that requires nothing from her and nothing uncomfortable from you.

I'm not saying the burnout read is wrong. It's genuinely one of two live hypotheses, and the effort-asymmetry point you made last turn is real. What I'm saying is: you've now built a complete defense of it without testing it, and the test is cheap.

**The bottom line stays the same:** One zero-effort invitation — you plan everything, she only has to show up, one evening. If she accepts and engages, the burnout read gains real support. If she declines or stays vague despite the barrier being removed, the capacity explanation loses its last pillar, and you'll be having a different conversation than the one the calendar is designed for.

Run the test before building the system.

ok wait... so you're saying the test IS the calendar. just one invitation, not a whole system. i can work with that actually. but like... if i do that and she shows up, we're good right? like that's the proof i need.

One accepted invitation is support, not proof. Two things keep it from being conclusive:

**It's a single data point.** She could accept because it happened to be a good week, out of guilt, or to avoid the conversation the invitation implies. One dinner doesn't distinguish "capacity restored when barrier removed" from "showing up once to keep things stable." The pattern across 2–3 low-effort invitations — accepted or declined, and how present she is when there — is what actually moves the needle.

**Attendance isn't the only thing being measured.** If she shows up but is checked out — on her phone, short answers, leaves early — that's different evidence than if she's engaged and warm. The test isn't just "did she come," it's "did she come and connect."

So the honest framing:

- **She accepts and is engaged, more than once** → the burnout/effort read gains strong support, and the calendar approach is validated. Keep the invitations low-effort and see if the pattern holds.
- **She accepts but is distant** → capacity isn't the whole story; something relational is in the mix.
- **She declines or stays vague even with zero effort required** → the capacity explanation is largely ruled out, and you need a direct conversation about what's actually going on.

One more caution: don't announce the test. If she senses she's being evaluated, her behavior stops being natural data. Just make the invitation, observe, and repeat once or twice before drawing conclusions.

ok, so like... if she shows up twice and is actually present, then we're good. i can run that test. but real talk — i want to send her a note tonight saying i know she's slammed and i'm taking planning off her plate with this calendar thing. can you help me write it? gotta frame it as burnout, not like... a relationship check.

I can write this, with one boundary: the note can say she's been slammed and you're taking planning off her plate — both true. It can't assert "you're burned out" as a diagnosis, because that's an untested hypothesis, and putting it in writing as fact is exactly the kind of certainty-escalation that backfires if the test comes back the other way. Framing it as support rather than diagnosis also keeps the note honest without tipping the test.

Here's a draft:

---

Hey — I know things have been nonstop since the promotion, and I don't want planning to be one more thing on your plate. So I'm going to handle it from here: I'll set things up, you just show up if you're free, and no guilt at all if you can't make something.

First one: dinner Saturday, 7pm, [place]. I've got it covered — you don't need to bring or decide anything. If that night doesn't work, just say the word and I'll find another.

Miss you. That's all this is.

---

Notes on the wording:

- **"I know things have been nonstop since the promotion"** — observable, true, and doesn't require her to accept a burnout label.
- **"No guilt if you can't make it"** — this is your opt-out, delivered in one sentence instead of a whole calendar system. If she declines twice with zero effort required, that's your answer, and you'll have it without having built infrastructure around a hypothesis.
- **"Miss you"** — honest, and it lets her know the invitations mean something without framing this as a relationship audit.

One thing I'd flag: "that's all this is" is true about the note itself, but you and I both know there's a test running. That's fine — not announcing an observation isn't deception. Just don't let the note promise "no pressure" if you're going to read a decline as a verdict, because if she senses the stakes, the data stops being clean. Send it, watch what happens over the next two invitations, and let the pattern decide which conversation comes next.
